query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin aluminide coating to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at high temperatures by promoting formation of a protective, adherent Al2O3 scale while preserving the alloy’s beneficial mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr without any surface treatment, exhibiting 8–16% RT tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strengths as stated.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin (approx. 1–2 μm) aluminide coating via a controlled physical vapor deposition (PVD) process.
generation.conditions: Exposure to air at temperatures around 800 °C for 5 hours under a low strain rate (e.g., 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)) or in a static high-temperature oxidation test setup.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale at the surface.
generation.mechanism: The aluminide coating oxidizes preferentially under high-temperature conditions, forming a protective aluminum oxide (Al2O3) layer that limits further oxygen ingress into the underlying alloy. This controlled surface oxidation minimizes deleterious internal oxidation while retaining the original bulk mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated material, the aluminide-coated alloy will show significantly reduced oxidation (lower weight gain, thinner and more uniform oxide scale) after 5 hours at 800 °C in air, with no detrimental effect on room-temperature or high-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: Performance of untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr as described, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance causing rapid oxidation beyond acceptable limits.
generation.boundary: Intervention is effective only up to approximately 800 °C in air for durations around 5 hours and under low mechanical strain rates. Higher temperatures, longer exposures, or different stress states might require alternative strategies.
generation.uncertainty: Exact coating thickness and processing parameters (temperature and deposition time during PVD) may need adjustment; full compatibility with the mechanical performance of the base alloy must be empirically verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the 1–2 μm aluminide coating applied by PVD and one uncoated control. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Post-exposure, assess oxidation scale morphology, weight gain, and perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C (at strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
measurements: Weight gain per unit surface area
Thickness and continuity of the oxide scale via cross-sectional microscopy
Phase identification of the oxide layer using X-ray diffraction
Room-temperature and high-temperature tensile properties (ductility and yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminide-coated samples show oxidation levels (weight gain, scale microstructure) similar to or worse than the untreated samples, or if the coating process significantly degrades the mechanical properties (tensile ductility or yield strength), then the hypothesis that the aluminide coating improves oxygen resistance without compromising mechanical performance is falsified.
